claims.text: The intervention is a systematic, moderate enrichment of Pt or Pd while holding all other synthesis parameters constant.
Increasing noble-metal content enhances the high-temperature structural stability of near-equiatomic multi-element solid-solution nanoparticles.
Increasing noble-metal content enhances the high-temperature chemical stability of these nanoparticles.
Noble-metal enrichment promotes a more uniform elemental distribution within the nanoparticles.
Noble-metal enrichment strengthens metal-metal bonding and increases atomic-level binding energy.
Stronger binding suppresses diffusion-induced elemental segregation.
Stronger binding suppresses nanoparticle sintering at high temperature.
Suppressing segregation and sintering maintains the solid-solution structure during high-temperature operation.
Noble-metal-enriched nanoparticles will have lower elemental-segregation rates than low-noble-metal baseline nanoparticles.
Noble-metal-enriched nanoparticles will have lower sintering rates than low-noble-metal baseline nanoparticles.
Reduced segregation and sintering will preserve catalytic properties during high-temperature operation.
Reduced segregation and sintering will preserve thermoelectric properties during high-temperature operation.
Low-noble-metal baseline nanoparticles undergo more pronounced segregation and sintering under high-temperature service conditions.
The proposed stabilization applies over 773–1173 K for catalysis and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric operation.
The effect is limited to moderate noble-metal adjustments that do not trigger a phase change or intermetallic-compound formation.
The effect is limited to compositions that remain uniform solid solutions.
The optimal noble-metal increment may depend on the specific combination of constituent metals.
A lack of statistically significant improvement in structural uniformity, sintering resistance, and performance stability relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
